name: Supply-shock propagation
causal_chain: A small number of suppliers account for most of an industry's critical input
An external shock (natural disaster, geopolitical disruption, demand spike elsewhere) removes capacity from that supplier base
Buyers relying on just-in-time inventory have no slack to absorb the gap
Production halts cascade downstream faster than new supply can be qualified or built
Recovery lags the shock by quarters to years because building new supplier capacity is slow

historical_instances.case: 2020-2023 global semiconductor chip shortage (automotive sector)
1973-74 OAPEC oil embargo -- concentrated exporter group's production cuts against a US oil industry with no spare capacity; embargo lifted March 1974 but prices stayed
historical_instances.source: Michael Corbett, 'Oil Shock of 1973-74', Federal Reserve History -- https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/oil-shock-of-1973-74

name: Prisoner's-dilemma price war
causal_chain: A small number of competitors serve the same customer base with substitutable products
One competitor cuts price to gain share, expecting rivals not to match
Rivals match the cut to avoid losing share, since matching dominates not-matching for each individual player
Industry-wide margins collapse below what any player would have accepted unilaterally
No player can unilaterally raise price back without losing share, so the low-price equilibrium persists until capacity exits

historical_instances.case: Delta Air Lines vs. Northwest Airlines Atlanta-Minneapolis hub price war

name: Regulatory-capture race
causal_chain: An industry has a small number of large incumbents who interact with the same regulator repeatedly
Incumbents invest heavily in lobbying, technical staff loaned to the regulator, and standard-setting participation
The regulator comes to rely on incumbent-supplied expertise and framing for technical rulemaking
Rules get written that favor incumbent technology/cost structure over new entrants or stricter alternatives
The incumbent's competitive position is protected by regulation rather than by superior product or price

historical_instances.case: German automotive industry's influence over EU vehicle emissions regulation

name: Platform envelopment
causal_chain: A platform provider has an established user base with existing network effects in market A
An adjacent market B has a separate incumbent whose product is a complement or weak substitute to the provider's
The provider bundles a B-market feature into its A-market platform at zero or near-zero marginal price
B-market incumbent's access to the shared user base is foreclosed, since users already have the bundled feature
The provider captures B-market share by leveraging A-market network effects, not by B-market product superiority

historical_instances.case: Microsoft bundling Internet Explorer with Windows (the 'browser wars')
historical_instances.source: https://www.ssrn.com/abstract=1496336 ; https://sms.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/smj.935 (Eisenmann, Parker, Van Alstyne, 'Platform Envelopment,' Strategic Management Journal, 2011)

name: Credit contagion
causal_chain: Financial institutions hold significant claims on each other's debt or collateral
One major counterparty fails or is perceived as likely to fail
Other institutions cannot verify their own exposure to the failing counterparty's exposure to others
Institutions hoard liquidity and cut interbank lending to protect against unknown exposure
Credit tightens system-wide even for institutions with no direct exposure to the original failure

historical_instances.case: Lehman Brothers bankruptcy and the collapse of interbank lending
Panic of 1907 -- run on Knickerbocker Trust cut off trust-company call-loan liquidity to NYSE brokers; annualized call-money rates spiked from 9.5% to 100% and runs spread across New York trusts
historical_instances.source: Jon R. Moen and Ellis W. Tallman, 'The Panic of 1907', Federal Reserve History -- https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/panic-of-1907

historical_instances.case: Caldwell and Company collapse, Nov 1930 -- failures cascaded through the correspondent-reserve pyramid, forcing hundreds of country-bank suspensions within weeks
historical_instances.source: Gary Richardson, 'Banking Panics of 1930-31', Federal Reserve History -- https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/banking-panics-1930-31

name: Ally drawn into a linked conflict
causal_chain: Two or more parties hold a formal mutual-support commitment (treaty, contract, alliance)
One party enters a conflict or dispute with a third party unrelated to the original commitment's purpose
The mutual-support commitment obligates the ally to escalate involvement, regardless of whether the ally's own interests are served
The ally's exposure and risk profile shifts to match a conflict it did not choose and may not benefit from
Disengaging costs the ally its credibility on every other commitment it holds

historical_instances.case: The European alliance system's cascade into World War I following Austria-Hungary's declaration on Serbia

name: Winner's-curse acquisition
causal_chain: An acquirer's own equity or currency is highly valued relative to its underlying fundamentals (a bubble or hype cycle)
The acquirer uses that inflated valuation as acquisition currency to buy a large target
Winning the deal requires outbidding rational estimates of the target's standalone value, since only the most optimistic bidder wins
Projected synergies used to justify the price do not materialize, since they were sized to justify the bid, not derived independently
The combined entity writes down goodwill once the valuation premise (the acquirer's own inflated price) reverts

historical_instances.case: AOL's acquisition of Time Warner ($182B, announced Jan 2000) and the subsequent $99B write-down (2002)

name: Debt-fueled capacity race
causal_chain: Multiple competitors in a capital-intensive industry each forecast continued demand growth
Each competitor debt-finances new capacity to avoid ceding future share to rivals doing the same
Aggregate capacity additions across all competitors outpace the real demand growth any one of them could see
Oversupply forces price/rate cuts industry-wide, below what services the debt taken on to build the capacity
The most leveraged competitor defaults first, but overcapacity (and depressed pricing) persists industry-wide after its exit

historical_instances.case: Hanjin Shipping bankruptcy amid container-shipping industry overcapacity (debt-to-equity ~850% at collapse)

name: Leverage-cycle bust
causal_chain: Households or firms increase borrowing against rising collateral values (home equity, asset prices) during an upswing
Rising leverage amplifies consumption and investment, which further inflates the asset prices used as collateral
A shock or plateau in asset prices halts the collateral-value increase that was funding new borrowing
Highly leveraged borrowers face margin/equity pressure and cut spending sharply to deleverage, since a small price decline wipes out a much larger fraction of thin equity
The resulting demand contraction and forced asset sales deepen the price decline, extending and worsening the downturn beyond what the initial shock alone would explain

historical_instances.case: US household leverage cycle and the 2007-2009 recession (home-equity-based borrowing amplifying the housing bust)
historical_instances.source: https://www.nber.org/papers/w15283 ; https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faer.101.5.2132 (Mian & Sufi, 'House Prices, Home Equity-Based Borrowing, and the U.S. Household Leverage Crisis,' American Economic Review, 2011)

name: Margin/collateral spiral
causal_chain: A highly leveraged position is financed via margin or derivatives (e.g. total return swaps) whose lenders can demand more collateral if the position's value falls
A price decline in the underlying position reduces its collateral value, triggering a margin call
The position holder cannot meet the margin call in cash and is forced to sell the underlying asset to raise it
The forced sale itself pushes the asset's price down further, since it is a large, price-insensitive sale rather than a valuation-driven one
The further price decline triggers additional margin calls (from the same or other lenders), repeating the cycle until positions are fully liquidated

historical_instances.case: Archegos Capital Management's forced liquidation of concentrated equity swap positions (Credit Suisse, Nomura, Morgan Stanley, and UBS all took losses)

name: Bank-run maturity mismatch
causal_chain: A bank funds itself with short-term, on-demand deposits while holding longer-duration assets (loans, held-to-maturity securities)
A rapid rise in interest rates reduces the market value of the bank's long-duration assets well below their face value
Depositors or analysts become aware of the resulting unrealized losses and question the bank's solvency
A subset of depositors, disproportionately concentrated or uninsured, begin withdrawing funds, forcing the bank to realize losses by selling assets at depressed prices to meet withdrawals
Realized losses confirm the solvency concern, accelerating withdrawals into a full run before the bank can raise capital or find a buyer

historical_instances.case: Silicon Valley Bank collapse -- $42B withdrawn in a single day following disclosed losses on its held-to-maturity securities portfolio, driven by 2022-2023 rate-hike-cycle duration losses

name: Carry-trade unwind
causal_chain: Investors borrow in a low-interest-rate funding currency and invest the proceeds in higher-yielding assets denominated in other currencies, profiting from the rate differential as long as the funding currency stays weak/stable
A policy surprise (e.g. an unexpected rate hike in the funding currency, or a rate cut in the target currency) narrows the yield differential and/or causes the funding currency to appreciate

Carry-trade positions become unprofitable or trigger losses on the currency leg, prompting leveraged holders to unwind (sell the target-currency asset, buy back the funding currency to repay the loan)
The unwinding itself pushes the funding currency higher and target-currency assets lower, since many holders are forced to unwind simultaneously

The self-reinforcing move (funding currency spikes, further squeezing remaining carry positions) transmits volatility broadly across asset classes financed by the same trade, not just the original currency pair

historical_instances.case: August 2024 global market selloff following the Bank of Japan's rate hike, unwinding an estimated multi-trillion-dollar yen carry trade (Nikkei -12.4% in a single day)
historical_instances.source: https://www.bis.org/publ/bisbull90.pdf (Bank for International Settlements, 'The market turbulence and carry trade unwind of August 2024')

name: Reflexive bubble (narrative-price feedback)
causal_chain: A compelling narrative about a transformative technology or trend takes hold among investors, unsupported yet by proportionate current fundamentals
Rising prices are read as confirmation of the narrative, not just sentiment, drawing in more capital and more believers

Companies and entrepreneurs respond to the availability of capital by launching more ventures fitting the narrative, which the market further rewards with rising prices, reinforcing the original belief
The feedback loop between narrative, price, and real investment decisions decouples valuations further from any current, verifiable fundamental

The loop breaks when new information (a prominent failure, a rate change, a growth disappointment) forces a reassessment; because the earlier rise was self-reinforcing, the reversal tends to be self-reinforcing too

historical_instances.case: The dot-com bubble -- internet-transformation narrative driving valuations far beyond current earnings/revenue support, 1999-2000, followed by the 2000-2002 crash
historical_instances.source: https://novelinvestor.com/reflexivity-explaining-bubbles/ ; George Soros, 'The Alchemy of Finance' (1987), the original statement of reflexivity theory

name: Monetary-tightening lag
causal_chain: A central bank raises its policy rate rapidly to combat inflation

Higher policy rates transmit to the real economy only gradually and unevenly -- through loan repricing, credit tightening, and investment/hiring decisions that take months to change -- the textbook 'long and variable lags' of monetary policy
Economic activity and inflation appear resilient in the near term even as the rate increases accumulate, since the lagged effects of earlier hikes have not yet arrived
The delayed effects of the full tightening cycle arrive together well after the policy rate has peaked, producing a sharper slowdown than the contemporaneous data suggested was coming
Because the slowdown appears after tightening has already stopped, it is frequently misread in real time as unrelated to the tightening cycle rather than as its delayed consequence

historical_instances.case: Volcker's 1979-1981 rate hikes (fed funds rate peaking near 22.4% in mid-1981) and the resulting July 1981-November 1982 recession

name: Sovereign-debt doom loop
causal_chain: Domestic banks hold large quantities of their own government's sovereign debt, often encouraged by favorable regulatory treatment
Concern about the government's fiscal position raises the market's perceived default risk, pushing sovereign bond yields up and prices down
The banks holding that sovereign debt suffer mark-to-market losses, weakening their own capital position and raising doubts about their solvency

Weakened banks either need a government-funded bailout (adding directly to the sovereign's debt burden) or restrict credit to the real economy (weakening growth and tax revenue, worsening the fiscal position indirectly)
Either channel further erodes confidence in the sovereign's finances, which further weakens the banks holding its debt -- a self-reinforcing loop between bank and sovereign credit risk

historical_instances.case: Greece and the eurozone periphery, 2010-2012 -- sovereign yield spikes and simultaneous domestic bank recapitalization needs, explicitly named the 'doom loop' in ECB/EU policy discussion

name: Capex overbuild
causal_chain: A new technology or transformative infrastructure category attracts genuine enthusiasm about future demand, distinct from deliberate multi-competitor racing (contrast debt_fueled_capacity_race)
Cheap capital and optimistic demand forecasts lead multiple independent builders to construct capacity sized to a shared, aggressively optimistic view of future demand
Actual demand grows more slowly than the capacity built to serve it, since the forecasts embedded a narrative premium rather than a measured trajectory
Realized utilization comes in far below what was underwritten, and prices for the resulting capacity (freight rates, bandwidth, whatever the capacity actually is) collapse under oversupply
The most leveraged/aggressive builders fail first, but the excess capacity itself persists and depresses prices/returns industry-wide for years after the initial building wave ends

historical_instances.case: US railroad overbuilding (33,000 miles laid 1868-1873) culminating in the Panic of 1873
Dot-com era fiber-optic telecom overbuild -- an estimated $2 trillion spent on 80-90 million miles of fiber, ~2.7% utilized by 2002, Global Crossing bankruptcy
historical_instances.source: https://www.richmondfed.org/~/media/richmondfedorg/publications/research/economic_quarterly/2003/fall/pdf/wolman.pdf (Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, 'Boom and Bust in Telecommunications')

name: Money-market contagion
causal_chain: Money market funds hold short-term debt (commercial paper, repo, financial-institution debt) and are widely treated by investors as cash-equivalent, redeemable at a stable $1.00 net asset value
One fund's holdings include debt of an institution that suddenly defaults or fails, causing that fund's net asset value to fall below $1.00 ('breaking the buck')
Investors in OTHER money market funds, unable to quickly verify their own fund's exposure to the same or similar risks, redeem preemptively rather than risk being caught in a second broken fund
The resulting wave of redemptions forces funds industry-wide to sell holdings and refuse to roll over commercial paper, even for issuers with no connection to the original failure
Short-term credit markets that rely on money-market-fund demand for commercial paper freeze, transmitting the shock to any borrower who depended on that funding channel

historical_instances.case: Reserve Primary Fund breaking the buck after Lehman Brothers' bankruptcy, triggering >$300B in prime money-market-fund redemptions

name: Debt-deflation spiral
causal_chain: An economy-wide buildup of debt occurs during a boom (over-indebtedness relative to income and collateral values)
A shock triggers debt liquidation: distress selling and repayment of bank loans contracts deposits and slows money velocity
The general price level falls as the money stock shrinks
Falling prices raise the real burden of every remaining unit of debt -- net worths and profits collapse faster than debts are repaid
The attempt to liquidate defeats itself: the more debtors pay, the more they owe in real terms
Output, trade, and employment contract; pessimism and hoarding further slow money velocity, deepening the deflation until mass bankruptcy or policy reflation breaks the loop

historical_instances.case: US Great Depression 1929-33 -- liquidation cut nominal debts ~20% while deflation raised the real debt burden ~40% (Fisher's own computation)
historical_instances.source: Irving Fisher, 'The Debt-Deflation Theory of Great Depressions', Econometrica 1(4) 1933 -- https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/meltzer/fisdeb33.pdf; Gary Richardson, 'Banking Panics of 1930-31', Federal Reserve History -- https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/banking-panics-1930-31

name: Input-cost inflation passthrough
causal_chain: A concentrated supplier group controls a critical, economy-wide input (energy, a key commodity)
Supply restriction or pricing power sharply raises that input's price while short-run demand is inelastic
The cost shock propagates through wholesale prices into consumer prices across every sector that uses the input
With the economy near capacity and inflation already elevated, the one-time price jump feeds wage- and price-setting expectations
Inflation shifts to a persistently higher regime while output slows -- a combination demand-management policy cannot offset on both sides at once

historical_instances.case: 1973-74 OAPEC oil embargo -- production cuts by the concentrated exporter group nearly quadrupled oil from $2.90 to $11.65/barrel in three months into an economy already running hot
historical_instances.source: Michael Corbett, 'Oil Shock of 1973-74', Federal Reserve History -- https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/oil-shock-of-1973-74; Blinder & Rudd, 'The Supply-Shock Explanation of the Great Stagflation Revisited', NBER w14563 -- https://www.nber.org/papers/w14563

name: Policy-tightening demand collapse
causal_chain: Inflation becomes entrenched in expectations after a period of accommodative or stop-go policy
The central bank tightens aggressively and holds policy tight despite rising unemployment, to restore credibility
Short rates rise above long rates as markets price eventual disinflation
Rate-sensitive, borrowing-dependent sectors (construction, manufacturing, autos) contract first and hardest
Unemployment rises sharply while inflation responds only with a lag
Once expectations break, inflation and long rates fall together and rate-sensitive demand recovers

historical_instances.case: Volcker disinflation and the 1981-82 US recession -- fed funds near 20%, unemployment peaking near 11%, inflation falling from ~11% (mid-1979) to 5% (Oct 1982)
historical_instances.source: Tim Sablik, 'Recession of 1981-82', Federal Reserve History -- https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/recession-of-1981-82; Goodfriend & King, 'The Incredible Volcker Disinflation', Journal of Monetary Economics 52(5) 2005
